title: 1 Samuel 14:1–15
context: 1 Samuel 14:1–15 tells of Jonathan’s bold attack on the Philistine garrison at the pass of Michmash. While Saul stays under a pomegranate tree at Gibeah with six hundred men and the priest Ahijah, Jonathan and his armor bearer secretly cross over. Jonathan’s confession, “there is no restraint on the LORD to save by many or by few,” is the theological center of the passage. He proposes a sign, the Philistines’ words fulfill it, and the two men climb up and strike about twenty of the enemy. The LORD then sends a great trembling and an earthquake on the Philistine camp. Both traditions read the episode as a narrative of faith and of the LORD’s saving power, not as a doctrinal dispute.

verses.text: Now it happened on a day that Jonathan the son of Saul said to the young man who bore his armor, “Come! Let’s go over to the Philistines’ garrison that is on the other side.” But he didn’t tell his father.
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan proposes to his armor bearer, “Come! Let’s go over to the Philistines’ garrison,” but he does not tell his father. Arminian readers note Jonathan’s initiative and courage. His faith expresses itself in action, in contrast to the paralysis and fear in Saul’s camp.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrative sets Jonathan’s initiative against Saul’s passivity and his secrecy against the formal structures of the camp. God is about to work through an unexpected agent. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing a story of faith and courage, and neither turns Jonathan’s venture into a doctrinal debate.

verses.text: Saul stayed in the uttermost part of Gibeah under the pomegranate tree which is in Migron; and the people who were with him were about six hundred men,
verses.arminianNotes: Saul stays “under the pomegranate tree which is in Migron” with about six hundred men. Arminian readers note the contrast between the king sitting still and his son going out to fight. The image suggests a leader who has lost initiative after Samuel’s rebuke.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the six hundred echo the count of 13:15, keeping before the reader how small and vulnerable Israel’s army is. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the contrast between Saul and Jonathan, and both see Israel’s weakness setting the stage for God’s deliverance.

verses.text: including Ahijah the son of Ahitub, Ichabod’s brother, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli the priest of the LORD in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. The people didn’t know that Jonathan was gone.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahijah, of the line of Eli and “Ichabod’s brother,” is with Saul, “wearing an ephod.” Arminian readers note that Saul keeps a priest at hand for inquiring of God, which suggests a real desire for divine guidance, even if he does not consistently follow it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reminder of Eli’s house, under judgment since 2:30, and of Ichabod, whose name recalls that “The glory has departed from Israel” (4:21). Shared ground: both traditions read the genealogy as connecting Saul’s camp with the troubled priesthood of Shiloh, and both note that the people did not know Jonathan had gone.

verses.text: Between the passes, by which Jonathan sought to go over to the Philistines’ garrison, there was a rocky crag on the one side and a rocky crag on the other side; and the name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh.
verses.arminianNotes: Between the passes stand two rocky crags, named Bozez and Seneh. Arminian readers note that the steep terrain makes Jonathan’s plan humanly improbable. The physical obstacles underline the courage required and the help Jonathan will need from the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator’s care with geography grounds the story in a real landscape and emphasizes the difficulty of the approach. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as background that magnifies the boldness of Jonathan’s act and the LORD’s work through it.

verses.text: The one crag rose up on the north in front of Michmash, and the other on the south in front of Geba.
verses.arminianNotes: One crag rises on the north in front of Michmash, the other on the south in front of Geba. Arminian readers note that the two crags frame the gap Jonathan must cross, placing him between the Israelite and Philistine positions in plain view of danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the precise description continues to set the scene, preparing for the climb in 14:13. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as descriptive detail, and neither finds a theological dispute in it.

verses.text: Jonathan said to the young man who bore his armor, “Come! Let’s go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that the LORD will work for us, for there is no restraint on the LORD to save by many or by few.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan says, “It may be that the LORD will work for us, for there is no restraint on the LORD to save by many or by few.” Arminian readers note the humble “It may be”: Jonathan trusts God’s power without presuming on his will. Faith acts boldly while leaving the outcome to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the confession of God’s unlimited power to save, which echoes the lesson of Gideon’s three hundred (Judges 7:2). Victory does not depend on numbers or weapons. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as common ground, teaching that salvation belongs to the LORD and that he is free to save by many or by few.

verses.text: His armor bearer said to him, “Do all that is in your heart. Go, and behold, I am with you according to your heart.”
verses.arminianNotes: The armor bearer answers, “Do all that is in your heart. Go, and behold, I am with you according to your heart.” Arminian readers note the loyalty and shared faith of Jonathan’s companion. His willing commitment makes him a true partner in the venture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase “according to your heart” echoes the language of the heart in 13:14, quietly contrasting faithful hearts with Saul’s. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a picture of loyal companionship in a God-centered venture, and both commend the armor bearer’s courage.

verses.text: Then Jonathan said, “Behold, we will pass over to the men, and we will reveal ourselves to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan says, “we will pass over to the men, and we will reveal ourselves to them.” Arminian readers note that Jonathan’s plan deliberately exposes him and his companion to danger. He does not rely on stealth alone but submits the venture to a test.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jonathan’s plan places the outcome in God’s hands. By revealing themselves, the two men make room for God to show his will. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Jonathan’s faith-filled approach, preparing for the sign in 14:9–10.

verses.text: If they say this to us, ‘Wait until we come to you!’ then we will stand still in our place and will not go up to them.
verses.arminianNotes: If the Philistines say, “Wait until we come to you,” Jonathan and his armor bearer will stay where they are. Arminian readers note Jonathan’s willingness to accept either answer. His faith is not reckless; he is prepared to stand down if God does not open the way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jonathan seeks a sign as an indication of God’s will, a practice the narrative presents without criticism in this case. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing a humble readiness to follow God’s leading, while noting that the narrative does not set this up as a general method for discerning guidance.

verses.text: But if they say this, ‘Come up to us!’ then we will go up, for the LORD has delivered them into our hand. This shall be the sign to us.”
verses.arminianNotes: If the Philistines say, “Come up to us,” they will go, “for the LORD has delivered them into our hand. This shall be the sign to us.” Arminian readers note that Jonathan expresses confidence in the LORD’s deliverance while still awaiting confirmation, holding faith and humility together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the language of deliverance as already accomplished, a recurring way Scripture speaks of God’s settled purpose in battle. Shared ground: both traditions read the sign as Jonathan’s way of seeking God’s direction, and both see the narrative affirming his faith by its outcome.

verses.text: Both of them revealed themselves to the garrison of the Philistines; and the Philistines said, “Behold, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they had hidden themselves!”
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines say, “Behold, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they had hidden themselves!” Arminian readers note the mockery, which recalls Israel’s hiding in 13:6. The enemy underestimates the two men, assuming they are as fearful as the rest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Philistines’ contempt sets up the reversal. God often works through those the world despises. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as heightening the irony of the scene, and both note the narrative link back to Israel’s fear in chapter 13.

verses.text: The men of the garrison answered Jonathan and his armor bearer, and said, “Come up to us, and we will show you something!” Jonathan said to his armor bearer, “Come up after me, for the LORD has delivered them into the hand of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: The garrison calls, “Come up to us, and we will show you something!” Jonathan says, “Come up after me, for the LORD has delivered them into the hand of Israel.” Arminian readers note that Jonathan acts on the sign at once. He claims the victory not for himself but for Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Philistines unknowingly speak the words of the sign, an instance of God directing even the speech of his people’s enemies. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the fulfillment of the sign and the decisive moment of Jonathan’s faith.

verses.text: Jonathan climbed up on his hands and on his feet, and his armor bearer after him, and they fell before Jonathan; and his armor bearer killed them after him.
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan climbs “on his hands and on his feet,” and the Philistines fall before him while his armor bearer finishes them. Arminian readers note the physical effort and risk involved. Faith does not remove the need for strenuous action; it moves the believer to act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the victory of two men over a garrison can only be explained by God’s help. The narrative highlights human weakness and divine power together. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a vivid picture of courage enabled by God, a pattern Scripture often repeats.

verses.text: That first slaughter, which Jonathan and his armor bearer made, was about twenty men, within as it were half a furrow’s length in an acre of land.
verses.arminianNotes: The first slaughter is “about twenty men, within as it were half a furrow’s length in an acre of land.” Arminian readers note the small scale of the initial victory, which nonetheless sparks a much larger rout. God can use a small act of faith to begin a great deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the measurement shows how confined the space was, magnifying the feat of two men. The number is modest, but the effect will be immense. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the start of the LORD’s deliverance, which spreads far beyond what Jonathan himself could accomplish.

verses.text: There was a trembling in the camp, in the field, and among all the people; the garrison and the raiders also trembled; and the earth quaked, so there was an exceedingly great trembling.
verses.arminianNotes: “There was a trembling in the camp … and the earth quaked, so there was an exceedingly great trembling.” Arminian readers note that God responds to Jonathan’s faith with a decisive act of his own. The trembling extends far beyond what two men could cause.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the earthquake and panic come from God; the Hebrew can be read as “a trembling of God,” though the WEB renders it “an exceedingly great trembling.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the LORD’s intervention, the turning point that makes the victory unmistakably his work.
